Read by that test and by frontend/src/constraint/render.test.ts, which is the second implementation these sentences pin.

vectors.name: built-scenario
vectors.note: Beat 3 of the built scenario, whole: the sentence the Trusted Surface shows and the user signs.
vectors.rendered: the amount is at most 200.00 USD and the time of purchase falls within 1 June 2026 and 31 August 2026 and the item's route origin is "beg" and the item's route destination is "pmi"

vectors.name: amount-cap
vectors.rendered: the amount is at most 189.00 USD

vectors.name: amount-under-one-unit
vectors.note: The zero-pad. A renderer that divided and trimmed would print 0.07 too, but one that sliced without padding prints .07 or crashes.
vectors.rendered: the amount is at most 0.07 EUR

vectors.name: amount-at-a-thousand
vectors.note: No thousands separator. Intl.NumberFormat gives $1,000.00 here, which is why the TypeScript renderer may not reuse formatAmount.
vectors.rendered: the amount is at most 1000.00 USD

vectors.name: amount-zero
vectors.note: A zero-amount authorisation is how an instrument is verified without charging it, so this is a real value and not an edge case.

vectors.name: amount-in-a-currency-with-no-minor-unit
vectors.note: A known limitation, pinned rather than fixed: renderMoney hardcodes two minor digits, so 189 JPY reads as 1.89 JPY where it should read as 189 JPY. Both renderers are wrong in the same way on purpose — the amount is never wrong, only its presentation, and the fix is a minor-unit table that contracts/instrument/amount.json already implies somebody will need. Do not make this vector agree with Intl, which gives the right answer here and the wrong one at amount-at-a-thousand.
vectors.rendered: the amount is at most 1.89 JPY

vectors.name: amount-negative-is-refused
vectors.note: A mandate authorises a payment; money moving the other way is a refund, which is a different object with a different authorisation. renderMoney carries a sign branch that no constraint can reach through Render — in Go it is reachable only through the rejection reason, where the subject's own amount is rendered.

vectors.name: money-list
vectors.note: Mixed currencies parse: which currency a purchase is in is not known when the mandate is signed, so the mismatch surfaces at evaluation and never here.
vectors.rendered: the amount is one of 200.00 USD, 100.00 EUR

vectors.name: money-band
vectors.rendered: the amount is between 100.00 USD and 200.00 USD

vectors.name: number-negative
vectors.note: The sign on a plain number, which money's zero-pad does not cover.

vectors.name: label-is-folded
vectors.note: Text values are normalised when the constraint is parsed, not when it is rendered. A renderer reading the raw JSON prints `  Flights  `.

vectors.name: label-is-folded-beyond-ascii
vectors.note: The fold is a full Unicode lower-casing in both languages, not an ASCII one.

vectors.name: item-identifier-keeps-its-case
vectors.note: item.id is exact. Whether two spellings name the same thing is the identifier scheme's business, and folding would decide it on the scheme's behalf.

vectors.name: identifier-with-surrounding-space
vectors.note: Even an exact identifier loses surrounding space: that is transport noise, not identity.

vectors.name: text-with-a-quote
vectors.note: Go renders text with %q and TypeScript with JSON.stringify; this is where the two would part company if either hand-rolled the escaping.

vectors.name: text-list
vectors.rendered: the item category is one of "flights", "hotels"

vectors.name: text-exclusion
vectors.rendered: the merchant category is not one of "casino"

vectors.name: item-attribute-noun
vectors.note: The noun comes from the addressed name with dots turned into spaces, and the value is folded like any other label.

vectors.name: item-attribute-noun-runs-deep
vectors.note: Every dot, not only the first. core does not know what a flight is, so an attribute name is whatever the mandate wrote.
vectors.rendered: the item's seat preference window is "aisle"

vectors.name: time-window
vectors.rendered: the time of purchase falls within 1 June 2026 and 31 August 2026

vectors.name: time-at-the-utc-day-boundary
vectors.note: The most valuable vector in the set. Go formats this instant in the zone it was parsed in, which for a Z timestamp is UTC, and says 31 August 2026. A TypeScript renderer reaching for new Date(x).getDate() reads the reader's own zone: east of Greenwich it says 1 September 2026 and the user is shown a window a day longer than the one they signed.
vectors.rendered: the time of purchase is before 31 August 2026

vectors.name: time-with-a-positive-offset
vectors.note: The other half of the same trap, and the half a machine in UTC would otherwise miss. The instant is 2026-08-31T22:30:00Z, so getUTCDate — the obvious fix for the vector above — says 31 August. Go says 1 September, because Format renders the wall clock in the offset the timestamp carried. No ambient timezone makes both this vector and time-at-the-utc-day-boundary pass a Date-based renderer: the first needs a non-positive offset and this one needs at least +01:30.
vectors.rendered: the time of purchase is before 1 September 2026

vectors.name: time-with-a-negative-offset
vectors.note: The same again from the other side: the instant is 2026-09-01T04:30:00Z, and the wall clock as written is 31 August.
vectors.rendered: the time of purchase is after 31 August 2026

vectors.name: time-single-digit-day
vectors.note: Go's `2` verb does not pad, so a renderer padding to two digits says 05 March.
vectors.rendered: the time of purchase is before 5 March 2026

vectors.name: time-with-a-fraction
vectors.note: Sub-second precision parses and then disappears: a user approving a booking window thinks in days.
vectors.rendered: the time of purchase is before 24 December 2026

vectors.name: time-list
vectors.rendered: the time of purchase is one of 1 June 2026, 1 July 2026

vectors.name: time-in-a-leap-year
vectors.rendered: the time of purchase is before 29 February 2028

vectors.name: either-of-three
vectors.rendered: either the item category is "flights" or the item category is "trains" or the item category is "coaches"

vectors.name: negation
vectors.rendered: it is not the case that the merchant category is "casino"

vectors.name: nesting
vectors.rendered: the amount is at most 500.00 USD and either the item category is "flights" or the item category is "trains"

vectors.name: nesting-at-the-limit
vectors.note: MaxDepth is 8 and the root is depth 0, so nine levels is the deepest thing that parses. The sentence is absurd; that it renders at all is the point.
vectors.rendered: it is not the case that it is not the case that it is not the case that it is not the case that it is not the case that it is not the case that it is not the case that it is not the case that the item category is "flights"

vectors.name: nesting-past-the-limit-is-refused
vectors.note: Ten levels. A verifier evaluates this on the request path against input it did not write, so the recursion is bounded by something other than good intentions — and the bound has to be the same number in both languages or one of them renders a constraint the other refuses.

vectors.name: unparsed-unknown-field
vectors.note: The registry is closed. `price` is not `amount`, and a renderer that guessed would show a limit the verifier rejects as constraint_type_unknown.

vectors.name: unparsed-operator-does-not-fit-the-field
vectors.note: Is Belgrade less than Palma has no answer anybody meant to ask, so ordering on text is refused when the mandate is read.

vectors.name: unparsed-group-with-no-children
vectors.note: `all` of nothing is vacuously true and would permit every purchase; `any` of nothing would refuse them all. Neither is something a person meant to sign.

vectors.name: unparsed-not-with-two-children
vectors.note: `not` over several children has two readings — none of them, or not all of them — and picking one silently would make a mandate mean something its author did not choose.

vectors.name: unparsed-inverted-range
vectors.note: An inverted range permits nothing, ever. Two values swapped is a far likelier explanation than an intent to authorise nothing.

vectors.name: unparsed-fractional-quantity
vectors.note: A count, not a measurement.

vectors.name: unparsed-quantity-as-a-string
vectors.note: Two wire representations of one claim means the looser arrives from whichever encoder was sloppiest.

vectors.name: unparsed-quantity-past-the-exact-integer-ceiling
vectors.note: 2^53. Above it a JSON number has already lost precision before either language saw it, and refusing loudly beats comparing something quietly wrong.

vectors.name: unparsed-amount-with-an-unknown-key
vectors.note: The unknown-operator rule one level down: a value carrying a key this verifier does not understand may not mean what the reader thinks it does.

vectors.name: unparsed-currency-not-iso-4217
vectors.note: The shape contracts/instrument/amount.json states, ^[A-Z]{3}$. Lower case is not merely untidy — accepting it here would make a renderer show a limit the verifier will not read.

vectors.name: unparsed-timestamp-is-a-date-only
vectors.note: RFC 3339, not ISO 8601's looser shapes.

vectors.name: unparsed-timestamp-with-lowercase-designators
vectors.note: RFC 3339 permits `t` and `z` in lower case; Go's time.RFC3339 layout does not, so this verifier does not either. A TypeScript regex written with the /i flag would accept it and render a limit Go refuses.

vectors.name: unparsed-item-attribute-with-no-name
vectors.note: `item.attr.` addresses nothing. The open half of the vocabulary is a rule, not an absence of one.
